name: Westinghouse Air Brake Technologies (Wabtec)

reads.name: What they do
reads.evidence: Makes locomotives, brakes, signalling, couplers and sensors for freight and transit rail, plus mining/marine/industrial gear, and then services the installed fleet for years; 2025 sales $11.17B.

reads.name: What they sell
reads.evidence: 2025 mix: Freight $8,036M (Services $3,055M, Equipment $2,365M, Components $1,586M, Digital $1,030M) and Transit $3,131M (OEM $1,393M, Aftermarket $1,738M). Freight Services plus Transit Aftermarket = $4,793M, 43% of sales (my calculation).

reads.name: Who buys
reads.evidence: Class I and other railroads, transit agencies, rail OEMs, miners; top five customers about 30% of 2025 sales, none above 10%. Moderate concentration; orders are lumpy (locomotives deliveries lower in Q3 2026).

reads.name: Where they operate
reads.evidence: 2025 sales: US $5,367M (48%), North America $6,192M (55%), Europe $1,956M, India $699M, Kazakhstan/CIS $431M (down from $559M in 2024), Australia/NZ $453M, South America $513M, Africa $326M (up from $194M). About 44.5% of sales are outside North America (my calculation), so a +4.8% 3-month dollar rise bites on translation. Hedges FX on acquisitions.

reads.name: Money model
reads.evidence: Razor-and-blade: sells locomotives and brakes once, then parts, modernisations and long service contracts for decades. Total backlog $31.4B (+22.9% y/y) but only $8.99B (29%) is 12-month backlog (+8.8%); Q3 sales of services booked as 'services' are only $493M of $3,120M (15.8%) at 40.8% gross margin vs 36.7% on goods (my calculation from the 10-Q).

reads.name: Operations
reads.evidence: Mostly variable material cost, adjusted op margin 22.9% (+1.9 pts) in Q3 2026; capex low ($182M 9M 2026, 1.5% of sales). Working capital heavy: inventory $2.95B vs customer deposits $0.80B (down from $1.02B), 9M customer deposits drained $149M. Guidance hit: raised 2026 adj EPS to $10.85-$11.05 (+$0.20). Long-contract revenue (over-time, estimate-based) is the auditor's critical audit matter.

reads.name: Supply chain
reads.evidence: Inputs: steel, aluminum, copper, rubber, energy, chemicals, polymers; 10-K says no long-term pricing with pure raw-material suppliers and some components are single-sourced (suppliers not named). Cost pass-through: price escalations and surcharges, but 10-K admits lags; Q3 10-Q says gross margin gains were 'partially offset by higher commodity costs and net tariffs' and tariff costs hurt 9M results with only a 'nominal' refund recovered. Linked to railroads signal tags capex, steel, dollar (industry value_chain row 'locomotives, signalling, track products'): steel/tariff cost is passed on only with a lag, while a stronger dollar lowers foreign sales. Adjusted gross margin still rose 1.8 pts, so pricing has so far beaten input cost.

reads.name: Edge
reads.evidence: Installed base in locomotives and brakes (one of two main US locomotive makers, with Progress Rail, per industry file; not re-verified), switching costs in signalling/train control, scale; Integration 3.0 targets $115-140M run-rate synergies by 2028. Differently now: digital (+24.2% in Q3, Frauscher sensors) and modernisations rather than new-build.

reads.name: Everyday brand
reads.evidence: Not a consumer brand (industry file everyday_brand false). Railroads would notice instantly if brakes and parts stopped, but no marketing-led pricing edge; R&D $223M in 2025 (2% of sales).

reads.name: Rivals and share
reads.evidence: Rivals: Caterpillar's Progress Rail (locomotives), Knorr-Bremse (brakes), Siemens/Alstom (signalling and transit). Share trend not disclosed; Q3 Equipment +0.3% with lower locomotive deliveries suggests no share surge in new-build.

reads.name: Growth runway
reads.evidence: Backlog $31.4B vs $25.6B a year earlier (+21.4% ex-FX); 2026 sales guide $12.3-12.6B (+11.5%) but Q3 organic only +4.7%, acquisitions +4.0%. Runway in India, Africa, Kazakhstan services, digital and modernisation; much of the multi-year backlog is long-dated.

reads.name: Cash and leaders
reads.evidence: FCF (CFO less capex): 2020 $648M, 2025 $1,499M; TTM about $1.78B (my calculation from XBRL). Q3 cash conversion 82%. Debt $6.38B, cash $0.49B, EBITDA about $2.8B, so net leverage about 2x; $1.7B of debt due within 12 months vs $2.09B liquidity. Goodwill $10.6B plus intangibles $4.0B of $23.1B assets, so after-tax return on capital is about 8% (my calculation), near the cost of capital. Buybacks $762M in 9M 2026 at much higher prices than 2024. Pay: adjusted EPS, cash conversion, 3-year ROIC and CFO, relative TSR. Insiders hold about 169,000 shares (0.1%, about $49M).

reads.name: Durability
reads.evidence: Rail is gaining relevance (freight and transit electrification, signalling mandates); services annuity on a long-lived fleet. Risks: Class I capex cycles, locomotive order timing, Kazakhstan/CIS volatility (sales -23% in 2025), customer concentration of top five at 30%. No sign of losing relevance.

reads.name: Red flags
reads.evidence: No 8-K Items 4.01/4.02/3.01, no NT filings, no CORRESP/UPLOAD letters found in EDGAR submissions 2018-2026; no material weakness. Watch items: GAAP EPS $6.86 vs adjusted $8.29 for nine months (17% gap, mostly amortisation and restructuring), a critical audit matter on estimates for over-time long-term contract revenue, and acquisition-heavy accounting ($1.06B spent on acquisitions in 9M 2026).

reads.name: Regime fit
reads.evidence: Boom: good (orders, capex). Overheat: good so far (price escalators, margin +1.9 pts) but the dollar +4.8% and tariff costs hurt. Stagflation: neutral (cost lags, but service annuity). Slowdown: backlog and aftermarket cushion earnings, but the multiple (35.7x GAAP trailing) and $6.4B debt would suffer with HY spreads widening and a Fed hike; orders from railroads fall in a freight recession.

reads.name: Rules and politics
reads.evidence: Exposed to US tariffs (net tariff cost a margin drag, refund claims pending) and steel/aluminum duties; non-US 44.5% of sales brings sanctions and trade risk (Kazakhstan/CIS, China $297M). Also exposed to FRA/PTC signalling rules (tailwind) and transit funding. No pending regulatory docket found for a Wabtec deal.

reads.name: Price
reads.evidence: At $287.59 (2026-11-25 close) EV is about $54.6B. Starting from owner FCF of about $1.7-1.9B (TTM, after SBC / adding back after-tax interest; my calculation), a 10% discount rate and 3% terminal growth need FCF growth of about 12-14% a year for 10 years. Own history: 12.3% a year 2021-2025 and 18.3% a year 2020-2025 from a depressed 2020 base, helped by acquisitions; Q3 organic sales growth is 4.7%. P/E 35.7x GAAP trailing and 26.3x on 2026 adjusted guidance ($10.95 mid) vs own year-end range 27.6x-31.1x (2021-2025, GAAP, my calculation); EV/EBITDA 19.7x vs TRN 13.0x, GBX 12.7x, FSTR 10.4x, CAT 16.9x. The price asks for a repeat of the best five years, so no cushion.

status_reason: Quality B but the price needs about 12-14% a year FCF growth for 10 years (same as its best five years), leaving no cushion, and no clear misreading found.

feedback.note: Customers/peers confirm demand but not an acceleration: AAR carloads +2.7% YTD and intermodal +5.1% YTD (Nov 21); Wabtec itself reports lower locomotive deliveries and lower North America railcar build in Q3.
Track and parts peer L.B. Foster Q3 sales +21.5% and new orders +35.7%, consistent with strong maintenance-of-way demand Wabtec cites.
Railcar maker Trinity cites steel tariffs and price-escalation clauses; Greenbrier says tariff uncertainty delayed long-lived railcar purchases: supports a tariff drag on railcar-related components.
